lead: The two budgets rest on two fiber numbers, attenuation and dispersion, and both must be measured on the fiber actually bought or laid. Attenuation is measured by the cut-back method on the bench and by an optical time-domain reflectometer (OTDR) on installed cable. Dispersion is measured in the time domain, from how much a pulse broadens, or in the frequency domain. Only a few syllabi teach these measurements in this detail.
prereq: You need fiber attenuation and dispersion, and the rise-time budget that uses them.

sections.h3: Total attenuation by the cut-back method

blocks.text: The cut-back method compares the power out of a long fiber with the power out of a short piece of it, with the launch untouched, so launch and detector cancel and the difference is the loss of the removed length.

items: Launch light at the test wavelength through a mode scrambler, so the modes are filled the same way every time.
Strip cladding modes at the far end and read P<sub>1</sub> through the full length L<sub>1</sub> on a large-area detector.
Cut the fiber about 2 m from the input and read P<sub>2</sub> through the short length L<sub>2</sub>.
Compute α; repeat at other wavelengths for a loss spectrum.

blocks.where: α is the attenuation in dB/km; P<sub>1</sub> and P<sub>2</sub> are the powers out of the long and the short length, in the same unit; L<sub>1</sub> and L<sub>2</sub> are those lengths in km.

blocks.text: Cut-back destroys fiber, so it suits the factory. For cable with connectors the insertion-loss method reads a reference through a short patch cord, inserts the cable and reads again; the difference includes the connectors.

An OTDR launches pulses into one end and records the Rayleigh backscatter against time. Light from distance z returns after t, so z = ct/(2n), with c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s and n the group index (about 1.47). The backscatter loses α going out and α coming back, so the raw trace falls at 2α; the display is halved, and its slope is α.
On the raw trace, α = 10 log₁₀(P(z1)/P(z2)) ÷ 2(z2 − z1). It needs one end only and also shows the splices and breaks used in the field tests.

sections.h3: Dispersion in the time domain and in the frequency domain

blocks.text: Time domain (pulse broadening). Record the half-maximum width of a narrow pulse at the input (τi) and output (τo). For near-Gaussian pulses the fiber's own broadening is τ = √(τo² − τi²) and its 3 dB optical bandwidth Bopt ≈ 0.44/τ. It suits multimode fiber.

Frequency domain (baseband response). Sweep a sinusoidal modulation and compare the received power through the long fiber and a short reference; the 3 dB (optical) point of the ratio is Bopt, with no pulse shape assumed.

Chromatic dispersion of single-mode fiber. The group delay τg is measured at several wavelengths, either as pulse arrival times (pulse delay) or as the phase of a sine wave modulated at fm (phase shift), where Δφ = 360° × fm × Δτ. Then D = (1/L) × dτg/dλ in ps/(nm·km). The phase-shift method needs no picosecond pulses and is the usual production method.

spec.aria: Two rows of the same set-up: source, mode scrambler, fiber, cladding-mode stripper and detector. Top row through 2.0 km of coiled fiber reads 6.3 microwatts; bottom row, cut to 2 metres, reads 20.0 microwatts. A dashed box around the source and scrambler says the launch is left untouched. The result line gives 2.51 dB per km.

examples.question: A cut-back measurement at 850 nm on multimode fiber reads 6.3 µW through 2.0 km. With the launch untouched, the fiber is cut to 2 m and the meter reads 20.0 µW. Find α and the total loss of the 2.0 km length.
steps: L<sub>1</sub> = 2.0 km and L<sub>2</sub> = 2 m = 0.002 km, so L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub> = 1.998 km.
Power ratio P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub> = 20.0 ÷ 6.3 = 3.175; loss = 10 log₁₀ 3.175 = 5.02 dB.
Total loss of the full 2.0 km: 2.51 × 2.0 = 5.02 dB (the 2 m stub adds only 0.005 dB).
Check: 2.51 dB/km is normal for multimode fiber at 850 nm.
examples.answer: α = 2.51 dB/km; the 2.0 km length loses 5.02 dB.

examples.question: A 0.4 ns (FWHM) pulse is launched into 2.0 km of graded-index fiber and leaves it 2.5 ns wide. Find the pulse broadening due to the fiber, the broadening per km, the 3 dB optical bandwidth and the bandwidth-length product.
steps: Bandwidth-length product: 178 MHz × 2.0 km = 357 MHz·km, a typical value for graded-index fiber.
examples.answer: τ = 2.47 ns (1.23 ns/km), B<sub>opt</sub> = 178 MHz and a bandwidth-length product of about 357 MHz·km.

traps: Dividing by L<sub>1</sub> instead of L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub>. The short piece was never part of the measured difference.
Taking the raw OTDR backscatter slope as α. Light goes out and back, so the raw slope is 2α; the displayed trace is already halved.
Subtracting pulse widths directly: 2.5 − 0.4 = 2.1 ns is wrong; widths subtract in quadrature.
The baseband response gives bandwidth; the phase shift against wavelength gives D.

quiz.q: Write the cut-back formula and name the two powers it compares.
quiz.a: α = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>) ÷ (L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub>); P<sub>1</sub> is the power through the full length, P<sub>2</sub> the power through the short cut-back length.

quiz.q: Why cut the fiber instead of disconnecting it and joining a short piece?
quiz.a: Cutting leaves launch and detector unchanged, so they cancel; a new joint adds an unknown loss.

quiz.q: On an OTDR's displayed trace, markers at 2.0 km and 4.0 km differ by 0.70 dB. Find α.
quiz.a: The display is one-way, so α = 0.70 dB ÷ 2.0 km = 0.35 dB/km, a normal value for single-mode fiber at 1310 nm.

quiz.q: A phase-shift set-up modulates the source at 500 MHz. Over 10 km of single-mode fiber the received phase changes by 122.4° when the wavelength steps from 1548 nm to 1552 nm. Find D.
quiz.a: Δτ = Δφ ÷ (360° × f<sub>m</sub>) = 122.4 ÷ (360 × 5 × 10⁸) = 680 ps. D = 680 ps ÷ (4 nm × 10 km) = 17 ps/(nm·km), the usual value of standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm.

quiz.q: Why does the phase-shift method avoid picosecond pulses and fast detectors?
quiz.a: It reads delay as the phase of a steady sine wave, which a narrowband receiver measures accurately.

quiz.q: Two cut-back readings on the same reel give 0.36 and 0.52 dB/km. The second operator re-cleaved and re-launched between readings. Which value do you trust, and why?
quiz.a: The 0.36 dB/km reading: re-launching changes the coupled power, adding an unknown term to one reading.

beyond: Factory benches step a tunable laser across the band and record loss, dispersion and polarization-mode dispersion of each reel automatically. Search for spectral attenuation measurement and PMD measurement.
